questions.questionText: Why can a model regression happen even when all standard unit tests pass?
options: It can't happen if unit tests pass
Unit tests typically check code correctness (types, no exceptions), which is a different question from whether the model's actual predictions are good
Unit tests always catch model quality issues
Model regressions only happen in untested code
questions.correctAnswer: Unit tests typically check code correctness (types, no exceptions), which is a different question from whether the model's actual predictions are good
questions.explanation: Code can run perfectly (no errors, correct types) while producing meaningfully worse predictions than before — which is why ML pipelines need model-specific evaluation checks beyond standard unit tests.

questions.questionText: What does an eval-set regression test in ML CI/CD actually check?
options: That the code compiles without syntax errors
That every model or prompt change is automatically scored against a fixed eval set, blocking deployment if the score drops meaningfully
That the training data file exists on disk
That the deployment server is reachable
questions.correctAnswer: That every model or prompt change is automatically scored against a fixed eval set, blocking deployment if the score drops meaningfully
questions.explanation: This automates the eval-set discipline from the NLP/LLM course's evaluation lesson, treating a meaningful score drop the same way a failing unit test would be treated — as a deployment blocker.

questions.questionText: Why does ML reproducibility require versioning data, not just code?
options: It doesn't, code versioning alone is always sufficient
A model's results depend on the exact dataset it trained on, and plain code versioning tools aren't naturally set up to track large dataset versions
Data versioning is only needed for image datasets
Reproducibility is impossible in ML regardless of versioning
questions.correctAnswer: A model's results depend on the exact dataset it trained on, and plain code versioning tools aren't naturally set up to track large dataset versions
questions.explanation: Since a model is a function of both code and the specific data it was trained on, truly reproducing a training run requires being able to point to the exact data version used, which needs dedicated tooling beyond typical code-focused version control.
